opening.headline: If we organize into a standard table which products and plans are allowed for each data level, how will the judgment that varies from case to case change?
body: The sales team wants to put customer lists into AI, the human resources team wants to put salary data, and the research team wants to put open papers into AI. The security team simply replies that it cannot be done because it is sensitive, and the business asks why other teams can do it but not us. Without a table linking data tiers to products and plans, decisions will vary on a case-by-case basis.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to group the previously covered preservation, use-for-learning, no-preservation, and special data conditions into a single rubric. The process of creating the framework of the table, filling in the columns with the provider's documents, distinguishing differences in settings using the condition column, and checking for omissions and contradictions is sequentially checked.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: You can match data levels with product/plan conditions.
Can determine omissions and contradictions in the standard table

screens.title: There are no standards for which products are allowed for each grade.
screens.lead: Read the three teams' requests and think about why each team gives different answers to the same question.

visual.alt: An illustration of the three teams' request cards and staggered response speech bubbles side by side.

paragraphs: Sales teams want to put their customer lists into AI to summarize them. The human resources team wants to find outliers in salary data, and the research team wants to organize published papers. This is a request that involves data of different sensitivities in the same AI product.

The security team simply answers that it cannot be done because it is sensitive, and other teams in the field do it, but ask why we cannot do it. The reason this conversation is repeated is because there is no table linking data tiers to products and plans. Without standards, the answer depends on the judgment of the person asking the question.
This lesson covers the structure of the table and how to read it. The table does not create new rules, but is a tool to organize conditions already in the provider document into in-house ratings.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Should the judgment be different if the settings are different for the same product? In the demo, see why you need condition columns.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our organization's data classification standards.

screens.title: Is there a standard for dividing data into grades?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. Since you will not submit an answer, first think about our organization.

items.prompt: Does my organization have criteria for categorizing data (public, internal, confidential, etc.)?
items.answer: Most classification criteria exist, but they are often not connected to the use of AI products. You can simply import existing grades to use as rows in the rubric. You do not need to create a new grade system.

items.prompt: Is that rating tied to permitted use of AI products?
items.answer: If it is not connected, it has a rating but is not being used. The table that links grades and products becomes the link.

items.prompt: Is there a process for updating tickets when product conditions change?
items.answer: A table is not a document you create once and then finish. It is necessary to write down the source document and the date of the version, and then re-check only the relevant column when the document is revised. Set a confirmation cycle so that the person in charge can take over even if the person in charge changes.

screens.outro: Now let's see how to create the framework of the rubric.

screens.title: Framework of the standard table: Grade × Product/Plan
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the process of filling out the rows, columns, cells, and condition columns of the rubric.

visual.alt: Skeleton illustration of a grid table where rows are data classes and columns are products and plans.

steps.title: row: data class
steps.body: Rows have in-house data ratings. Existing classifications such as public, internal, confidential, and special (regulated) are used. It is easier for readers to write in our organization's language without importing the provider's classification.

steps.title: Column: Products and Plans
steps.body: Columns contain product and plan units separated by provider documents. Units such as Personal App, Team or Enterprise, API Standard, API No Retention, and HIPAA Readiness Plan. Even products from the same company have different retention and learning usage conditions, so they are divided by product and plan, not by company.

steps.title: Khan: allowed, conditional, prohibited
steps.body: In each box, write one of the following: allowed, conditional, or prohibited. Cases that are neither permitted nor prohibited are conditional, and those conditions are explained in separate columns. Writing long sentences in the box makes it difficult to read, so keep the verdict to one word.

steps.title: condition column
steps.body: In the Condition column, write down the items that are prerequisites for permission. Examples include learning enablement settings, retention period, processing region, agreement (BAA or no retention), and available features. Even for the same product, if these conditions are different, different judgments will be made.

steps.title: principles of structure
steps.body: The higher the grade, the narrower the range of products allowed. Products that are Accepted in the top row require additional conditions to appear Accepted in the bottom row. This principle later becomes the basis for checking omissions and contradictions.

screens.outro: Now that we've created the framework, let's fill in the blanks based on the provider's documents.

screens.title: Fill in the fields with supporting documents
screens.lead: The table below is an example of the range of products allowed by grade and the basis for it. Read which document and under what conditions the decision for each line was made.

data.notes: If the rationale column for each row is empty, the decision will not be confirmed but will be put on hold. The URL of the supporting document and the date it was read are recorded next to the table. This way, people reading the table can follow the evidence and check it for themselves.

screens.outro: Let's check why the condition column is needed by comparing it with the allowed characters.

screens.title: Maintain condition columns and rubrics
screens.lead: Click the toggle to compare how the judgment of the same column changes in tables without and with condition columns.

states.label: No condition column
states.body: If you just write Allow in the box, the list of settings that need to be turned on disappears. For example, it is written that internal data is allowed in a corporate product, but if an employee uses the same product with a personal account, it is read as allowed because it is the same product. Plans where the organization does not specify a retention period are also read as permitted. Since there is no way to distinguish between two situations with different settings, the table does not help you make a decision, and you end up asking again for each case. Conversely, if you read the table too strictly and treat all boxes as prohibited, business will find a route to bypass the table. The condition column allows for a realistic decision between allowable and prohibited.

states.label: Has condition column
states.body: If there is a condition column, even for the same product, different judgments will be made if the settings are different. The default for OpenAI Enterprise is to disable learning, but there is little documentation that retention control varies from product to product, so move this to the condition column. The table includes the URL of the source document, the date of the version read, and the identifier. When the product conditions document is revised, a procedure is in place to recheck only the relevant column, so that it remains up-to-date without having to create a new table. When the product conditions document is revised, a procedure is in place to recheck only the relevant column, to maintain the current status without having to create a new table. With a checker and confirmation date, you can pick out old fields at a glance.

screens.outro: Now let's look at an explanation of how the permitted products narrow as the grade increases.

screens.title: Explanation: The higher the grade, the narrower the allowable products are.
screens.lead: Move the slider to increase your data level. You can see how the range of acceptable products decreases as you move up the tier.

stops.body: Public press releases are allowed for all products. Whether you put it in a personal app, business, or API, there is a low risk of information leaking. However, conditions remain. Check your learning settings and double-check that the material is truly public. Acceptable product areas are all four prongs. At this stage, conditions are the mildest, but not without conditions.

Internal meeting minutes are allowed in enterprise and APIs, but prohibited in personal apps. This is because consumer accounts are beyond the organization's control, as conversations can be used for training and stored in de-identified form for up to five years, depending on model improvement settings. The range of acceptable products is reduced to three branches:

Customer personal information is conditionally accepted only on plans with retention settings and regional options for Enterprise. Organizations need to be able to set retention periods and specify processing locations so they can respond to deletion and access requests. Long-term storage exceptions in case of safety violations are also written in the Conditions column. The range of accepted products is reduced in two.

Medical records are only accepted on HIPAA ready plans and products with a BAA. No preservation alone is not enough; only functions covered by BAA should be used, excluding out-of-scope interfaces such as Console. The key to this structure is the narrowing down of the permitted product range. You can understand that each time the level goes up, one more condition is added, and the number of products that meet the conditions decreases.

screens.outro: Now that we have seen the structure, let's see how to find omissions and contradictions in an already created table.

screens.title: Commentary: Finding Omissions and Contradictions
screens.lead: When you select an item, the error and the rationale for fixing it will be displayed. First, think about what went wrong and then check. A contradiction is when the columns in the table do not match, and an omission is when a condition that should be present is missing.

items.prompt: Contradiction: Special tier says personal apps are allowed
items.answer: Consumer plans are contradictory because they are outside the scope of no-retention and HIPAA preparation. The special class personal app section should be changed to prohibited, and the corresponding document should be written in the justification column.

items.prompt: Missing: API no-preservation column exists, but no conditions for functions to which no-preservation does not apply
items.answer: No Preservation does not apply to features that are No in the eligibility table, so the condition column must state that the feature is turned off or restricted. Otherwise, the no-preservation column will read wider than it actually is.

items.prompt: Missing: Area condition field for classified level is empty
items.answer: The confidentiality level requires conditions on inference location and storage location. If the processing area is determined by regulation or contract, write down the regional options for the product. If there are no options, leave it as prohibited.

items.prompt: Contradiction: There is a sentence that says special data is allowed if there is no preservation.
items.answer: Because no-preservation and HIPAA readiness are separate commitments, no-preservation alone cannot allow for special data. Fix it to require a HIPAA prepared plan and BAA.

Check each row for supporting documentation, working from top to bottom to see that the allowances become narrower as the level increases. It is a contradiction if there is a cell that allows the bottom row to be wider than the top row. Checks are conducted both when new tables are created and when supporting documents are revised.

screens.outro: Now that you've learned how to check the table, let's summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Rubrics put conditions in columns
screens.lead: Summarizes the contents of this class.

paragraphs: A benchmark is a grid of data levels, products, and plans. Write Allowed, Conditional, and Prohibited in the boxes and place the conditions in a separate column. The higher the grade, the narrower the allowable products should be.

Omissions and contradictions are checked in two ways. Look at each row for supporting documents, scanning from top to bottom to see if the limits are narrowing. If the product terms and conditions are revised, please leave the supporting documents and version date so that you can check only the relevant box.

Rubrics do not replace judgment, but are a tool to make judgment consistent. Rubrics do not eliminate human judgment. If you receive a request for a new product or new grade that is not in the table, judge it in the same way by increasing the columns and rows of the table. This way, you can respond to each request by updating the table rather than debating it anew. And if you leave the reason for the change and the date each time you update a column in the table, you can later explain why the decision was changed.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The word allow must be followed by the conditions under which it is allowed.

checks.intro: Check out for yourself what the condition column does. This confirmation is not logged.
checks.q: What problems will arise if I only write ‘Allow’ in the column of the standard table and do not include a condition column?
options: It loses track of which settings should be turned on, making it impossible to distinguish between the same product with different settings.
The order of grades is reversed.
The supporting document cannot be found
checks.explain: Even for the same product, the judgment varies depending on learning usage settings, retention period, etc., so conditions must be written in a separate column.

wrong.0: If a condition is omitted, it does not become stricter, but rather leaves the basis for judgment empty.
wrong.2: Rank order is a matter of row organization and is not directly related to the condition column.
wrong.3: Supporting documents are separated into URL and date columns.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. If there are no conditions, two situations with different settings are mixed in one space.
checks.incorrectFeedback: What happens when a condition is missing is not the strength or order of the decision. Think about what makes a difference in the same product.

checks.intro: Arrange them in order to see how the allowed products narrow as the data level increases.
checks.q: Arrange them in the order in which the allowed products become narrower as the data level increases.
items: Public press release: All products accepted
Customer privacy: Only enterprise plans with retention/locality options are allowed conditionally
Medical Records: Only products with HIPAA ready and BAA accepted
checks.explain: The core structure of the standard is that as the level increases, the allowable products are reduced to areas 4, 3, 2, and 1.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. We have implemented a well-established structure in which the allowable range narrows as the grade increases.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. Think of a flow from the tier with the most acceptable products to the tier with the fewest.

glossary.def: This is an in-house classification based on the sensitivity of the data, such as public, internal, confidential, and special.
It is a combination of products and plans approved for use by level.
This is a column where you write down items that are prerequisites for permission, such as learning settings, preservation, region, and contracts.
This is a procedure to write down the supporting document and edition date and re-check only the relevant fields when revising.

misconceptions.fact: If a condition is missing, the results for the same product will vary depending on the settings.

misconceptions.myth: The highest grade can be the most expensive product.
misconceptions.fact: Conditions such as conservation, location, and contract must be met. Conditions are the standard, not price.

misconceptions.myth: Once you create the table, you are done.
misconceptions.fact: When product conditions are revised, we check them again.

closing.lead: We recapitulate the key points of this lesson.
points: The standard is a grid that connects grades and products/plans.
The higher the grade, the narrower the products allowed.
Maintain tables with source documents and edition dates.
